primary_topics: Address at a book launch for Jose T. Almonte's 'We Must Level the Playing Field,' August 16, 2007 -- with President Fidel V. Ramos as special guest

CJP's personal tribute to FVR: first met in 1983 at Rotary Club of Manila; the June 17, 1992 one-on-one meeting; the offer of Justice Secretary (declined), then SC; FVR never spoke to CJP about any case -- 'Such is the gentleman that he is'

Portrait of Jose T. Almonte (JoeAl): initially feared as James Bond/Napoleon Solo combined; eventually revealed as 'a true-blue ideologue, thinker, philosopher, strategist, reformer, visionary and patriot'

The book's central thesis: 'We Must Level the Playing Field' -- cut the networks of collusion; smooth economic distortions; give everyone a fair and equal chance; lift the poor only through economic growth that creates jobs
sub_topics: Public thanks to FVR: 'May I publicly say maraming salamat po, President FVR, for initiating me into public service and for appointing me to the Supreme Court on a Double Ten, October 10, 1995'
First meeting with Ramos: 1983, both new members of the Rotary Club of Manila

June 17, 1992 meeting: early morning one-on-one in FVR's private office; discussed many topics; offered Justice Secretary (declined -- 'I had neither campaigned for him nor supported his candidacy... I had voted for my mentor, Senator Jovito R. Salonga'); FVR then offered the SC (accepted as non-partisan)

FVR's gentleman quality: 'Though I owe my appointment to the Supreme Court solely and completely to him, he never spoke to me about any case or matter pending in the Court since then. Such is the gentleman that he is.'

First impression of JoeAl: 'because of his intelligence background, I thought of him as some sort of James Bond and Napoleon Solo combined. Behind the stony facade, however, is a very kind person, gentle of spirit and loyal to a fault to his true friends.'

JoeAl's influence on CJP's judicial philosophy: 'his commonsensical theories strengthened my own belief that law could not be read in a vacuum. It must be interpreted and applied in the context of pulsating contemporary social and economic realities. The rule of law must not only safeguard liberty but must help eradicate poverty and nurture prosperity.'

Book title as ideology: 'We Must Level the Playing Field' summarizes the author's ideology; direct quote from JoeAl: 'To level the playing field of enterprise, we must cut the networks of collusion that have allowed persons of influence to extract wealth without effort from the economy. And we must smooth the economic distortions that perpetuate jobless growth and uneven development.'

JoeAl on the poor: 'instead of dole-outs and charity, he posits that the poor can be lifted up only by economic growth that creates and expands jobs and business opportunities for all those willing to take them.'
Governing conclusion: 'President Fidel V. Ramos may have been the embodiment of Philippines 2000 but National Security Adviser Jose T. Almonte was the sentient soul of the Ramos Presidency'

stances.claim: President Fidel V. Ramos was the embodiment of Philippines 2000 as a public figure and program; but Jose T. Almonte was 'the sentient soul of the Ramos Presidency' -- the intellectual engine who shaped the vision of leveling the playing field, rooting out collusion networks and achieving prosperity through economic growth rather than dole-outs. The president was the face; the NSA was the mind.

stances.claim: FVR's most telling quality is not his governance record but his personal integrity: appointed CJP to the SC knowing he didn't campaign or vote for him, and then never spoke to him about any pending case. This is the specific behavioral evidence that makes FVR 'such a gentleman' -- not general praise but two specific acts.

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered August 16, 2007 at the launch of Jose T. Almonte's 'We Must Level the Playing Field' -- with President Fidel V. Ramos as special guest -- this address by CJP opens with public gratitude: 'maraming salamat po, President FVR, for initiating me into public service and for appointing me to the Supreme Court on a Double Ten, October 10, 1995.' He narrates their history: first met in 1983 at the Rotary Club of Manila; on June 17, 1992, FVR offered Justice Secretary (CJP declined -- 'I had neither campaigned for him nor supported his candidacy... I voted for my mentor, Senator Salonga'); FVR replied he wanted to be President 'not only of those who voted for me but also of those who did not, but who are competent and honest' and offered the SC instead; FVR then never spoke to CJP about any pending case -- 'Such is the gentleman that he is.' He turns to Almonte: initially feared as 'some sort of James Bond and Napoleon Solo combined'; eventually discovered as 'a true-blue ideologue, thinker, philosopher, strategist, reformer, visionary and patriot' whose commonsensical theories reinforced CJP's belief that 'law could not be read in a vacuum. It must be interpreted and applied in the context of pulsating contemporary social and economic realities. The rule of law must not only safeguard liberty but must help eradicate poverty and nurture prosperity.' The book's thesis (quoted directly from Almonte): 'To level the playing field, we must cut the networks of collusion that have allowed persons of influence to extract wealth without effort from the economy... smooth the economic distortions that perpetuate jobless growth and uneven development.' On the poor: 'they can be lifted up only by economic growth that creates and expands jobs and business opportunities, not by dole-outs and charity.' Conclusion: 'President Fidel V. Ramos may have been the embodiment of Philippines 2000 but National Security Adviser Jose T. Almonte was the sentient soul of the Ramos Presidency.'
